deep.reconstruction:
The page is a set of tables of biquadratic (quartic) residue classes for the primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) from 101 to 149. The next page continues the series (157, 173, 181, 193) and then tabulates the class of +3 and -3. Each block has the same structure.

Header 'p, g, f, a+bi':
- p is the prime.
- g is a primitive root mod p.
- f is the square root of -1 mod p given by f ≡ g^((p-1)/4).
- a+bi is the Gaussian prime factor of p with a²+b² = p, normalized so that a ≡ 1 (mod 4), b is even, and a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p); equivalently a f ≡ b. Under this normalization, i ↦ f in Z[i]/(a+bi) ≅ F_p.

The five header cases:
- p=101, g=2: f = 2^25 = 10 (mod 101), 10² = 100 ≡ -1; 101 = 1²+10²; 1 + 10·10 = 101 ≡ 0.
- p=109, g=6: f = 6^27 = 33; 33² = 1089 ≡ -1; 109 = 3²+10²; -3 + 330 = 327 = 3·109.
- p=113, g=3: f = 3^28 = 98; 98² ≡ -1; 113 = 7²+8²; -7 - 784 = -7·113.
- p=137, g=3: f = 3^34 = 100; 100² ≡ -1; 137 = 11²+4²; -11 - 400 = -3·137.
- p=149, g=2: f = 2^37 = 105; 105² ≡ -1; 149 = 7²+10²; -7 + 1050 = 7·149.

Rows A, B, C, D: the residues 1..p-1 are partitioned by ind_g(x) mod 4. Equivalently, the classes are defined by x^((p-1)/4) ≡ 1, f, -1, -f. This is exactly the A/B/C/D classification of Gauss's Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum I (1828). A is the set of biquadratic residues. Each class has (p-1)/4 members; the counts on the page are 25, 27, 28, 34 and 37, all correct.

Spot checks (mine):
- p=149: the powers 2^(4k) mod 149 are 16, 107, 73, 125, 63, 114, 36, 129, 127, ..., all listed in A.
- p=137: 4, 16, 64, 81 and 3^8 = 122 are in A. 2, 8, 9, 32, 128 and 44 (= 3^6) are in C. 27 and 3^7 = 132 are in D. 3^5 = 106 is in B.
- -1 = p-1 lies in C when (p-1)/4 is odd (101, 109, 149) and in A when it is even (113, 137), as listed.

These tables serve as the empirical basis for the biquadratic character of small numbers, from which Gauss induced biquadratic reciprocity.
- Class of 2: 2 lies in B, B, A, C, B for b/2 = 5, 5, -4, -2, 5, i.e. classes A, B, C, D correspond to b/2 ≡ 0, 1, 2, 3 (mod 4). This is Gauss's 1828 theorem on the quartic character of 2.
- Class of 3: 3 lies in B (101), A (109), B (113), B (137), D (149). These entries feed the '+3 | -3' tally on the next page, and they match it.
errors: No errors found in the header data (f, g, a+bi) or in the spot-checked class memberships.

results.what: Complete tables of quartic residue classes (index mod 4 relative to f = g^((p-1)/4)) for p = 101, 109, 113, 137, 149
results.modern_name: Quartic residue character / biquadratic residue symbol tables

results.what: Normalization of the Gaussian prime a+bi | p with a ≡ 1 mod 4, b even, a f ≡ b (mod p), linking i to f
results.modern_name: Choice of Gaussian prime factor compatible with the reduction map Z[i] -> F_p (near-primary normalization)

results.what: Data consistent with the class of 2 being determined by b/2 mod 4
results.modern_name: Supplementary law for 2 in quartic reciprocity

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of exactly the kind Gauss used for biquadratic residues in 1828-1832. The classification, the normalization and the use of the data (characters of 2 and of ±3) are well known as his. This is a neat confirmation of his working method, not a new result.
